content.p: On 19 December 2024 a criminal court in Avignon, in southern France, found Dominique Pelicot guilty of the aggravated rape of his then-wife Gisèle and sentenced him to 20 years in prison, the maximum for rape under French law. Over nearly a decade, he had drugged her, filmed the assaults and invited strangers he met online to rape her while she was unconscious. Fifty other men were tried with him, and all were convicted, with sentences from three to 15 years.

Pelicot admitted the offences, including at trial. He did not appeal, so his sentence is final. The case became known worldwide because Gisèle Pelicot refused anonymity and insisted that the trial, and the videos that proved it, be public.

Dominique Pelicot, 72 at the time of the trial, is a retired electrician and estate agent, the Guardian reported. He and Gisèle, his wife of 50 years, had retired in 2013 to the village of Mazan in Provence. They have three children, David, Caroline and Florian. Gisèle sang in a choir and liked country walks. She has since divorced him. During the trial she said she had thought she was in a loving marriage and had never found anything strange about the food and treats he brought her.

Between 2011 and 2020, Pelicot told the court, he mixed sedatives into her food and drink so that he could rape her, and recruited at least 50 other men through an online chat forum to do the same. The Guardian wrote that he used a chatroom on the unmoderated site Coco, in a room called "Against her knowledge", and that he archived videos of more than 200 rapes in a folder on his hard drive. ABC reported that he kept 20,000 photos and videos. Gisèle Pelicot testified that she had no memory of the events and had spent years wondering why she was so tired.

On Saturday 12 September 2020, a security guard at a supermarket in Carpentras, about 20 minutes from Mazan, saw Pelicot filming up women's skirts with a hidden camera and called the police, according to the Guardian. At the station, officers who heard him describe an "urge" took a closer look at the chat history on the two phones he was carrying, then searched his home. Police found thousands of photos and videos on his drives, CBS reported, and they led to the other suspects.

The Guardian reported that Pelicot had come to police attention before: in 2010 he had been caught filming up women's dresses in a supermarket in the Seine-et-Marne area and accepted a fine of 100 euros to avoid court. The paper said his DNA, taken after that arrest, matched a trace from the scene of a 1999 attempted rape of a young estate agent, but the match never reached the case file at the time. After his 2020 arrest the cold case was reopened, and the paper reported that when confronted with the DNA in 2022 he admitted an attempted rape but denied using a knife.

The trial opened on 2 September 2024 and lasted more than three months. Several defendants asked for the hearings to be held behind closed doors. Gisèle Pelicot opposed that, and the court sided with her. "I have nothing to be ashamed of. Shame must change sides," she said on the opening day. She insisted that the videos be shown in court. In October she told the court she wanted all women who are victims of rape to say to themselves, "Madame Pelicot did it, so we can do it."

Dominique Pelicot told the court that he was guilty and that his co-defendants knew exactly what they were doing. "I am a rapist like the others in this room," he said. He asked his family to accept his apologies. His co-defendants largely disagreed. ABC reported that most denied intending to rape her and claimed Pelicot had tricked them. None disputed the sexual acts, but many said they thought it was a fetish game or that Gisèle had consented. Some others acknowledged wrongdoing.

On 25 November prosecutors asked for the maximum 20 years for Pelicot. For most of the other defendants, ABC said, they asked for 10 years or more, while AFP gave a range of 10 to 18 years for those facing aggravated rape charges.

The five judges delivered their verdicts on 19 December. Arata told him, "Mr Pelicot, you are found guilty of the aggravated rape of Gisele Pelicot". He was also found guilty of attempting to rape the wife of one of his co-accused, a woman, and of taking indecent pictures of his daughter and of his two sons' wives, CBS reported. He showed no emotion as the verdicts were read.

The reports count the verdicts differently, across all 51 defendants including Pelicot. Al Jazeera said 47 were guilty of rape, two of attempted rape and two of sexual assault. CNN said 49 were guilty of rape and two of sexual assault, noting that its post had been updated to correct the number found guilty of rape, and Global News said one man accused of rape was convicted of sexual assault instead. The reports agree that all 51 were convicted of something. Sentences ranged from three to 15 years, and two were suspended. CNN reported that the most prosecutors had sought for all the men together was 652 years, against 441 years imposed in total.

The Guardian profiled the convicted men. Jean-Pierre Maréchal, a former lorry driver, was not accused of raping Gisèle Pelicot. He was sentenced to 12 years for drugging and raping his own wife by the same method, and for organising Pelicot's rape of her too. Romain Vandevelde was sentenced to 15 years for raping Gisèle Pelicot on six occasions between 2019 and 2020. Husamettin Dogan, who denied the charge, received nine years. A man named Cocco was convicted of sexually assaulting her and sentenced to three years, two of them suspended. A defendant named Ouamou was tried in absentia and sentenced to 12 years.

Many campaigners and Gisèle Pelicot's children were disappointed. A family member told AFP that the children were "disappointed by these low sentences". Catherine Le Magueresse of the European Association Against Violence Toward Women told CNN she was "surprised by the leniency", and a source close to the case told CNN the judges may have varied the sentences to limit appeals. Outside the court Gisèle Pelicot said she respected the decision, that she would "never regret" her decision to open the trial to the public, and that she was thinking of the "unrecognised victims whose stories often remain in the shadows".

Every defendant had 10 days to appeal. By 30 December, Global News reported, Pelicot's lawyer, Béatrice Zavarro, had told France Info that he would not appeal, to spare his former wife another ordeal. She conceded that a new trial before a public jury could produce a longer sentence. Seventeen of the co-defendants initially lodged appeals, but all but one later withdrew them.

The remaining appellant was Husamettin Dogan, 44, a construction worker who had received nine years. He argued that Pelicot had deceived him and that he never meant to rape her. His retrial began on Monday 6 October 2025 in Nîmes and was meant to take four days at most, with judgment due that Thursday. He remained free until the verdict. Gisèle Pelicot returned to court and was applauded when she arrived, although her lawyer Antoine Camus said she would have preferred to stay out of it.

Dominique Pelicot testified as a witness at the appeal. He said Dogan had been a willing participant and had known his wife would be asleep. An investigator told the court that Dogan's account was contradicted by the footage, which showed him present for at least 3 hours and 24 minutes, not the half an hour he claimed. From the night of Dogan's 2019 visit to the couple's home, AFP said, investigators recovered 107 photos and 14 videos from Pelicot's hard drive. Civil proceedings were set for November in Avignon to settle the damages owed jointly by the convicted men to Gisèle Pelicot and her family.

The trial triggered protests across France, and some demonstrators hoped that it would lead to changes in French law on consent. CBS noted that French law defines rape through violence, coercion, threat or surprise rather than through the absence of consent, so prosecutors have to show intent. Gisèle Pelicot is now widely seen, CBS said, as an emblem of resistance to sexual violence, in France and elsewhere.
